title: Items
text:
Selecting the Item ID will take you to a page displaying the question, answer, and (if available) worked solutions and other notes.
Clicking the Stem can be used to quickly preview a question, but may not show all elements (e.g., graphs, mathmatical text, etc.).
The TXT column shows the question and answer in raw text format for easy copying and pasting.
The Export checkbox allows instructors to mark questions for export and generate a consolidated plain-text file for easy copying into an Canvas. Because the export is just raw text, images are not included.
The R Exam column provides the item’s R Markdown code for any instructors using the “exams R package”. This package enables you to do things like:

Randomize question order and question elements (e.g., values, names, etc.)
Display corresponing graphs, and other diagrams
Generate multiple exam versions automatically
Export exams to different formats (Canvas, Word documents, Webpages, PDFs, and more)

Note: This approach requires solid knowledge of R and the exams package.

title: Item 8
text:
Include in export 

What happens to the sample standard deviation of the values below if 100 is added to each of them?
0.05, -0.42, -0.84, -2.04, -0.2, 0.24, 0.79, 2.46, -0.86, 1.3, 2.56, 1.8, -0.08, -1.51

The standard deviation is multiplied by 100
The standard deviation has 100 added to it
The standard deviation stays the same
The standard deviation has 100 subtracted from it
The standard deviation is divided by 100


Correct Answer
FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE


Solution:
Adding a constant to all values in a dataset does not change the standard deviation.
The standard deviation measures the spread or variability of the data around the mean. When you add a constant to every value, you shift all the data points by the same amount, which shifts the mean by that same amount. However, the distances between each data point and the mean remain unchanged.
We can verify this with the data:
x <- c(0.05, -0.42, -0.84, -2.04, -0.2, 0.24, 0.79, 2.46, -0.86, 1.3, 2.56, 1.8, -0.08, -1.51)

sd(x)        # Original SD
sd(x + 100)  # SD after adding 100
Both standard deviations are equal to 1.4026
Therefore, the standard deviation stays the same.

title: Item 6
text:
Include in export 

The following histogram depicts the distribution of defence points for all of the Pokemon characters (up to generation VII) in the popular video game franchise Pokémon. According to the esteemed Pokémon Database, defence points, “measure the ability to take attacks from other Pokémon; the higher the stat is, the fewer Hit Points will be lost when attacked.”



Histogram of Pokémon Defence Point Values


Using inequalities (i.e., greater and less than symbols > <), choose the option that best describes this distribution:

Mean < Median > Mode
Median > Mode > Mean
Mode > Median > Mean
Mean > Median > Mode
Median > Mean > Mode


Correct Answer
FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE


Solution:
Extreme values on the right side will pull the mean towards the right the most, followed by the median, and then the mode.
Values on the right side of the x-axis have a larger numerical value than values on the left.
In a right-skewed distribution like this one, the mean is pulled most strongly by extreme values, making it the largest measure of central tendency, followed by the median, then the mode.
Thus, the answer is: Mean > Median > Mode

title: Item 4
text:
Include in export 

A researcher had five different groups of rats in an experiment. Each group of rats was given a different dosage of caffeine. The number of rats in each group and their dosage in milligrams (mg) is below. What was the mean dose of caffeine across all the rats?



Group
Rats
Dose




Control
14
0


A
9
4


B
11
8


C
6
16


D
15
32




Correct Answer
12.72727


Solution:
The mean dose is 12.73 mg (rounded to two decimal places).
This is a weighted mean problem, where each dose is weighted by the number of rats receiving that dose.
The formula is: \[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}\]
Calculating: \[
\begin{align}
\bar{x}
&= \frac{14 \times 0 + 9 \times 4 + 11 \times 8 + 6 \times 16 + 15 \times 32}{14 + 9 + 11 + 6 + 15} \\[0.5em]
&= \frac{0 + 36 + 88 + 96 + 480}{55} \\[0.5em]
&= \frac{700}{55} \\[0.5em]
&= 12.727\overline{27}
\end{align}
\]
R code:
x <- c(0, 4, 8, 16, 32)   # doses in mg
w <- c(14, 9, 11, 6, 15)  # number of rats (weights)

weighted_mean <- sum(x * w) / sum(w)
weighted_mean

title: Item 2

Include in export 

\(\Phi\) is a very sacred number called the “Golden Ratio”. Some people believe that it has magick properties which allow us, mere mortals, to understand more than just the natural world. It is approximately equal to:
1.6180339887498948482045868343656381177203091798057
Including the 1 preceding the decimal, what is the mode of the first 21 digits of \(\Phi\)?

Correct Answer
8


Solution:
Counting the frequency of each digit, the most frequently occurring digit is 8, therefore the mode is 8.

title: Item 1
text:
Include in export 

A student scored the following percentages on their end of the year exams:

Alchemy: 47
Astrology: 32
Falconry: 37
Logic: 89
Music: 56
Swordsmanship: 35
Tarot: 46
Xylomancy: 34

What was their mean score?

Correct Answer
47


Solution:
The mean score is calculated as:
\[\frac{\sum x}{N} = \frac{47 + 32 + 37 + 89 + 56 + 35 + 46 + 34}{8} = \frac{376}{8} = 47\]
R Code:
x <- c(47, 32, 37, 89, 56, 35, 46, 34)
mean(x)

title: Item 3
text:
Include in export 

Which of the following is a valid way to label a sample mean? Select all that apply.

\(\sigma\)
\(\bar{x}\)
\(\bar{y}\)
\(\hat{x}\)
\(\mu\)


Correct Answer
FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE


Solution:
The correct answers are \(\bar{y}\) and \(\bar{x}\).
Sample means are denoted using bar notation (e.g., \(\bar{x}\) or \(\bar{y}\)), where the bar over the variable indicates the mean of the sample data.
Why the other options are incorrect:

\(\mu\) (mu) is the symbol for the population mean, not the sample mean. Greek letters are reserved for population parameters.
\(\hat{x}\) (x-hat) typically represents a predicted or fitted value in regression analysis, not a sample mean. While both are estimates, they serve different purposes.
\(\sigma\) (sigma) is the symbol for the population standard deviation, not a measure of central tendency.

Key distinction: Sample statistics use Roman letters with special notation (like the bar), while population parameters use Greek letters.

title: Item 5
text:
Include in export 

Destinee rolled two six-sided die and plotted their values on the histogram below. What percentage of the rolls were either a 6, 7, or 8?


Correct Answer
35


Solution:
Each bar shows the number of times a certain value was rolled. Therefore the total percentage of rolls for 6, 7, and 8 is . . .
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Percent} &=
\frac{2+1+4}{1+2+3+1+2+1+4+2+2+2} \times 100 \\[0.5em]
&= \frac{7}{20} \times 100 \\[0.5em]
&= 35.00
\end{align}
\]

R Code:
freq_678 <- c(2, 1, 4)
freq_tot <- c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 4, 2, 2, 2)

sum(freq_678) / sum(freq_tot) * 100

title: Item 7
text:
Include in export 

The mean of two numbers is 639.5, and one number is 37 more than the other. What is the value of the smaller of the two numbers?

Correct Answer
621


Solution:
We can solve this with some basic algebra where \(x\) is the smaller of the two numbers:
\[
\begin{align}
\frac{x + (x + 37)}{2} &= 639.5 \\[0.5em]
\frac{2x + 37}{2}      &= 639.5 \\[0.5em]
2x + 37                &= 639.5 \times 2 \\[0.5em]
2x                            &= (639.5 \times 2) - 37 \\[0.5em]
x                             &= \frac{(639.5 \times 2) - 37}{2} \\[0.5em]
x                             &= 621
\end{align}
\]

Using the data file pearson_lee_1903.csv, convert the children’s heights into centimetres (the data file has them in inches). Then calculate the mean height of all the children.
Note: 1 in = 2.54 cm

Correct Answer
167.7142933


Solution:

heights <- read.csv("pearson_lee_1903.csv")

# Convert values to cm and calculate mean
result <- mean(heights$child * 2.54)
